title: ECG foundation models for cardiovascular screening in a cohort of young competitive athletes
desc: AI-powered cardiac screening could evolve sports medicine by boosting accuracy, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness, with automated ECG interpretation based on foundation models becoming key for large-scale athlete screening. Before deployment, it is crucial to verify whether these clinically developed models are applicable to this population. We evaluated whether ECG foundation models trained on general clinical populations can diagnose athlete-specific ECG findings. We fine-tuned three models (ECG-FM, HuBERT-ECG, ECGFounder) on PhysioNet/CinC 2021, 87,662 samples, and tested them on 43 expert-annotated ECGs from highly trained/national-level athletes. Performance was strong on PhysioNet/CinC 2021 (AUROC 0.97, AUPRC 0.57, Sensitivity 0.89) but dropped on athletes’ data, confirming domain shift. ECGFounder performed best (AUROC 0.84, AUPRC 0.72, Sensitivity 0.57) and detected the most frequent findings, Sinus Bradycardia (AUROC 0.87) and Sinus Arrhythmia (AUROC 0.95), well. Per-label estimates for rare classes must be interpreted cautiously, given the small cohort. This work contributes to developing athlete-focused AI frameworks for reliable ECG-based screening.

title: A global atlas of digital dermatology to map innovation and disparities
desc: Artificial intelligence promises democratized access to dermatological care, but model reliability depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of the underlying data. Despite rapid growth in publicly available dermatology images, the field lacks quantitative indicators to measure whether new datasets expand clinical coverage or merely replicate what is already known. Existing collections are widely assumed to be biased, yet the scale and topography of these gaps have remained unquantified, leaving the community without a road map for strategic data acquisition. Here, we show, by unifying 1.1 million images from 29 public datasets into a queryable semantic atlas, that the global archive is markedly skewed and increasingly redundant: darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick V–VI) constitute only 11.0% of images, pediatric patients only 2.3%, and informational novelty has plateaued despite exponential growth, revealing where targeted data acquisition is most needed.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Screening and Early Detection of Prostate Cancer.
desc: [European urology focus] Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming prostate cancer screening and early detection through the integration of clinical-risk calculators, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), digital pathology, genomics, biomarkers, and liquid biopsies. AI-enhanced risk models may improve biopsy decisions, while AI-assisted MRI interpretation can increase the detection of clinically significant disease and reduce false positives, unnecessary biopsies, and overdiagnosis. Digital pathology algorithms may support more reproducible tumor identification, Gleason grading, and prognostic stratification. Genomic risk scores, kallikrein-based tests, and emerging circulating biomarkers further enable precision screening by identifying men at elevated risk and refining the selection for imaging or biopsy. However, most available systems address isolated components of the diagnostic pathway, and evidence from prospective, real-world screening populations remains limited. Clinical implementation therefore requires external validation, screening-specific calibration, implemented reference standards, and workflow integration. Ultimately, multimodal AI may enable a "virtual biopsy" that combines imaging, molecular, pathological, and clinical data to deliver personalized, noninvasive prostate cancer assessment.

Accelerating high-throughput catalyst screening by direct generation of equilibrium adsorption structures
desc: The adsorption energy serves as a crucial descriptor for the large-scale screening of catalysts. Nevertheless, the limited distribution of training data for the extensively utilised machine learning interatomic potential, predominantly sourced from near-equilibrium structures, results in unreliable adsorption structures and consequent adsorption energy predictions. In this context, we present DBCata, a deep generative model that integrates a periodic Brownian-bridge framework with an equivariant graph neural network to establish a low-dimensional transition manifold between unrelaxed and DFT-relaxed structures, without requiring explicit energy or force information. Upon training, DBCata effectively generates high-fidelity adsorption geometries, achieving an interatomic distance mean absolute error of 0.035 Å on the MamunHighT2019 dataset from Catalysis-Hub, which is approximately 70% lower than that of the current state-of-the-art machine learning potential models. Moreover, the corresponding DFT accuracy can be improved within 0.1 eV in 94% of instances by identifying and refining anomalous predictions through a hybrid chemical-heuristic and self-supervised outlier detection approach. We demonstrate that DBCata enables accelerated high-throughput computational screening for alloy catalysts in the oxygen reduction reaction, highlighting the potential of DBCata as a powerful tool for catalyst design and optimisation.

title: Potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence to address disparities in epilepsy.
desc: [Nature reviews. Neurology] The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and health care offers unprecedented opportunities to address global disparities in access to specialized epilepsy diagnosis and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advances in AI models, combined with increasing internet connectivity and smartphone usage in low-income and middle-income countries, offer promising solutions for epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring through AI-based analysis of electroencephalography recordings captured with affordable open-source systems, smartphone data and electronic health records. However, this technological revolution raises important questions about the preservation and expansion of clinical expertise, AI algorithm transparency and health-care equity. In this Review, we examine how AI can help to address disparities and improve global epilepsy care while maintaining high clinical standards and addressing systemic challenges.

Artificial Intelligence in Thoracic Pathology and Biomarker Assessment: An IASLC Pathology Committee Review.
source: PubMed · Journal of thoracic oncology : official publication of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer
desc: [Journal of thoracic oncology : official publication of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer] Artificial intelligence (AI) is starting to transform pathology by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, prognostication, and therapeutic prediction through advanced computational analysis of histopathological images. This review explores key AI methodologies and their applications in lung cancer diagnostics. Supervised learning dominates current clinical AI tools, relying on annotated whole-slide images (WSIs) for tasks like tumor subtyping, quantitation of tissue-based parameters, prediction of driver alterations (e.g. EGFR and KRAS mutations, ALK rearrangement), and assessment of tumor microenvironment (TME) features. Meanwhile, weakly supervised and self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, such as multiple instance learning (MIL) and contrastive learning, reduce dependency on labor-intensive annotations and uncover novel prognostic morphologic patterns. AI demonstrates strong performance in predicting therapeutic responses, including immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy, while emerging techniques like spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence further leverage AI to decode complex spatial biology and generate novel biomarkers. Despite much progress, major challenges persist in validation, reliability, interpretability, regulatory approval, ethics and data privacy standards, cost and reimbursement, equity, and integration into clinical workflows. Adoption requires scalable digital pathology infrastructure, interdisciplinary collaboration, and suitable reimbursement frameworks. Regulatory efforts aim to address ethical and safety concerns, but global harmonization remains incomplete. We also consider the professional consequences of adoption, including cognitive deskilling, workforce displacement, and the conditions under which pathologist oversight remains meaningful rather than nominal, and argue that liability should follow the reality of control. As AI evolves, particularly with foundation models and large language models (LLMs), thoracic pathology stands to benefit from substantially extended diagnostic and predictive capabilities, pending resolution of implementation barriers.

Individual Probability of Successful Extubation Using a Neural Network: A Proof-of-Concept Analysis.
desc: [Rhode Island medical journal (2013)] Studies have shown that artificial intelligence can aid in extubating patients from ventilators, but none have used predominantly respiratory parameters to yield a simple probability of successful extubation that can immediately aid clinicians in their decision to extubate or not extubate patients. We sought to determine whether it is possible to create a neural network as a proof-of-concept analysis using predominantly respiratory parameters to derive a single probability of successful extubation for an individual patient. Fourteen predominantly respiratory parameters were the input for a neural network with one hidden layer to yield a single output, a simple probability of extubation. The system trained on 17 patients, 13 of whom successfully extubated, four of whom failed. The results showed excellent separation between the extubation successes and failures. When applied to the test group of four patients, there also was excellent separation between the three successful extubations (prediction range: 98.8% to 100% probability) and the one failure (2.9% probability). This proof-of-concept analysis showed that it is possible to use predominantly respiratory parameters to present a single number, a probability of extubation, as the output from a neural network. This analysis needs to be performed on a larger sample before it can be applied confidently, but the framework now is available for further development to assist intensivists who work with ventilated patients.

Evaluating the Accuracy of an Artificial Intelligence Solution Program for Identifying Anatomical Landmarks in Orthodontics.
desc: [Healthcare informatics research] This study quantitatively evaluated the accuracy and clinical reliability of EzOrtho, deep learning software designed to identify anatomical landmarks automatically for orthodontic diagnosis. Real-world clinical data were used to assess its applicability in practice. We analyzed 23 lateral cephalometric radiographs. EzOrtho automatically identified 36 anatomical landmarks per radiograph, yielding 828 data points for comparison with ground truth established by experienced orthodontists using a standardized annotation protocol. Accuracy was quantified using mean radial error (MRE), and clinical reliability was assessed using the successful detection rate (SDR), defined as the percentage of all points within the clinically acceptable threshold of 2.0 mm. The overall MRE was 0.78 mm, and the SDR at the 2.0 mm threshold was 86%. Although most landmarks were detected precisely, the landmark-specific analysis identified higher error rates at a few points in anatomically complex regions, indicating areas for improvement. The findings suggest that EzOrtho may offer clinical utility and reliability for automatic cephalometric landmark detection using real clinical data. Its performance indicates the potential to improve efficiency and consistency relative to manual tracing. However, the study's limitations, including its small sample size, mean that these results remain preliminary. Further validation is needed to establish its role as a decision-support tool in orthodontic practice.

title: Progress in the Application of Artificial Intelligence in Radiotherapy: From Image Guidance to Adaptive Radiation Therapy.
source: PubMed · Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
desc: [Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)] Radiotherapy plays a crucial role in cancer management, integral to curative approaches for 45%-50% of malignancies. However, conventional workflows face significant challenges, including operational inefficiency, inter-observer variability, and limited personalization. This review describes the evolutionary trajectory of artificial intelligence (AI) applications within the domain of radiotherapy, with a principal focus on the cardinal paradigm shift from image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) toward adaptive radiotherapy (ART). AI has demonstrably improved both the precision and efficiency of radiotherapy. This stems from its application across several critical areas: automating complex tasks in medical image analysis-like segmenting tumors, enhancing real-time motion management with the ability to capture target displacements down to the submillimeter level; and providing sophisticated decision support systems to aid clinicians. Within the sphere of ART, online adaptive systems leveraging magnetic resonance linear accelerators (MR-Linacs) and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) facilitate dynamic target delineation, dosimetric re-optimization, and cumulative dose assessment. These capabilities forge a closed-loop system based on "perception-decision-execution," effectively shifting radiotherapy beyond static planning and -toward truly personalized, dynamic treatments.

title: Impact of MRI sequence heterogeneity on deep learning-based segmentation of brain metastases.
desc: [PloS one] Brain metastases (BMs) require accurate delineation for treatment planning, yet magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) acquisition protocols vary substantially in clinical practice. Such protocol-level heterogeneity may affect the generalizability of deep learning-based segmentation models. This study evaluated the impact of heterogeneous T1-weighted MRI protocols on BM segmentation performance using two three-dimensional architectures, 3D Attention U-Net and DUCK-Net 3D. A retrospective dataset of 925 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI studies from 720 patients was analyzed. Models were trained under six sequence configurations, including multi-sequence, Black-Blood (BB), Non-Black-Blood (Non-BB), and three single-sequence cohorts. Independent test datasets consisted of three MRI cohorts: MPR Range, MPR Thick Range, and T1 SPACE 3D. Five-fold cross-validation was performed. Performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), volumetric regression, and false discovery rate-corrected statistical comparisons. DUCK-Net 3D demonstrated more consistent performance across independent MRI cohorts, particularly under cross-sequence conditions. Multi-sequence training achieved the most stable cross-sequence performance, whereas single-sequence models showed greater sensitivity to protocol variability. Segmentation accuracy declined for small lesions (<0.4 mL) across both architectures. These findings suggest that MRI protocol heterogeneity affects segmentation performance and that sequence-diverse training may improve cross-sequence robustness in clinical settings.

title: Evaluating readability of AI-generated pediatric dental education materials.
desc: [Frontiers in digital health] General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have become a popular source of oral health information. However, the patient education materials (PEMs) generated by these models often pose readability challenges. This study aimed to: (1) compare the readability of PEMs generated by six AI chatbots in response to ten frequently asked questions on pediatric oral health; and (2) determine whether the readability of these texts meets the level recommended by the American Medical Association (AMA). Ten sample questions on pediatric oral health were compiled. Each question was submitted once to each of six AI chatbots (GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2.5, and Qwen3-Max), generating a corpus of 60 texts in a blocked (repeated-measures) design. Six readability indices - Flesch Reading Ease (FRE), Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Gunning Fog Index (GFI), Coleman-Liau Index (CLI), Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG), and Automated Readability Index (ARI) - were calculated for every text. Each index was analysed separately using the Friedman test, with the ten questions as blocks and the six models as conditions, followed by Dunn's multiple comparison test. Kendall's coefficient of concordance (W) was calculated to quantify the consistency of model ranking across questions. DeepSeek-V3 showed the highest readability (easiest texts) and Gemini 3 Flash the second highest, whereas Claude Haiku 4.5 showed the lowest readability across all six indices; GPT-5 Mini, Qwen3-Max, and Kimi K2.5 occupied intermediate positions. All six Friedman tests were statistically significant (χ 2(5) = 31.77-35.94, all p < 0.0001), and Kendall's W ranged from 0.635 to 0.719, indicating that the relative ranking of the six models was broadly consistent across the ten questions. Against the AMA-recommended sixth-grade reading level, all models exceeded the recommended difficulty on every index; even against a more lenient seventh-grade threshold, only the ARI median of DeepSeek-V3 (6.5) fell below 7. The PEMs generated by the six LLMs were written at a reading level above the AMA recommendation, and reading difficulty differed systematically among models. Readability should be explicitly controlled through prompt design, model optimisation, and professional review before such materials are used in pediatric oral health education.

title: A Clinically Weighted Transformer-Based Deep Learning Model for Automated FLIP Panometry v2.0 Interpretation.
source: PubMed · Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association
desc: [Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association] Functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) Panometry evaluates esophageal motility by measuring contractile responses and esophagogastric junction opening, but interpretation requires expertise and varies between readers. We aimed to develop a transformer-based deep learning model for automated FLIP Panometry v2.0 interpretation, incorporating a clinically weighted cost matrix that penalizes clinically consequential errors. 984 adults who underwent FLIP Panometry and high-resolution manometry (HRM) were included. Expert FLIP Panometry v2.0 interpretation, assigned blinded to HRM, served as the reference standard for training and evaluation. HRM (Chicago Classification v4.0) characterized the cohort and corroborated expert FLIP labels. Inconclusive or discordant HRM studies were excluded. A transformer model with a weighted cost matrix was evaluated on a held-out test set using the six-category FLIP Panometry v2.0 scheme and grouped binary ("normal" vs "not normal") and three-class ("normal," "abnormal," "obstructive") schemes. The model reproduced expert six-category classification in 83.5% of test studies (95% CI 76.4-88.7%). Binary accuracy was 94% (89-97%), with 97% sensitivity (91-99%) and 89% specificity (76-95%). Three-class accuracy was 89% (83-93%); sensitivity and specificity for obstructive patterns were 93% (82-97%) and 96% (90-99%). No normal studies were classified as obstructive, or vice versa. Versus an unweighted baseline model, cost-sensitive training was associated with 15% lower aggregate misclassification cost (95% CI -16% to 39%). A transformer-based model reproduced expert FLIP Panometry v2.0 interpretation with high agreement in a selected single-center cohort. Accuracy was numerically higher than prior convolutional models trained on different data. These findings support a potential role for AI-assisted FLIP interpretation, but external validation is required before clinical use.

title: Generative AI adoption is more widespread than predictive AI at US hospitals.
desc: [Health affairs scholar] Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among U.S. hospitals has accelerated rapidly, yet national estimates of predictive and generative AI implementation across clinical and administrative settings remain limited. Using data from 2203 nonfederal acute care hospitals in the 2025 American Hospital Association Information Technology Survey, we described AI adoption, model source (electronic health record [EHR] developer, third-party developer, or self-developed), and specific clinical and administrative use cases. We assessed associations between hospital and area characteristics and AI adoption, model source, and number of AI use cases using weighted multivariable regression. In 2025, 81% of hospitals reported using AI, with 77% of hospitals using generative AI-more than double the rate reported in 2024. The most common applications were ambient documentation (73%) and predicting health trajectories or risks (70%). System affiliation and use of the market-leading EHR were the strongest predictors of AI adoption. Hospitals using EHR-developed AI reported 2.48 additional AI use cases (95% CI, 1.93-3.03). Generative AI adoption surpassed predictive AI for the first time, driven by ambient documentation. While use of EHR-developed AI was associated with greater use, there was a greater influence of third-party vendors for generative AI compared to predictive AI. Continued monitoring will be essential to assess AI's impact across healthcare.

Exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers: Biological principles, fabrication strategies, characterization, and therapeutic applications.
source: PubMed · Nanomedicine : nanotechnology, biology, and medicine
desc: [Nanomedicine : nanotechnology, biology, and medicine] Biomimetic nanocarriers inspired by exosomes have emerged as a transformative strategy for precision drug delivery by combining the biological advantages of naturally derived extracellular vesicles with the scalability and tunability of synthetic nanotechnology. Native exosomes exhibit intrinsic immune evasion, membrane stability, ligand-mediated cellular tropism, and the ability to traverse complex biological barrier properties that conventional nanocarriers have struggled to replicate. This review systematically discusses the biological basis of exosomes, including their biogenesis, molecular composition, and intercellular communication roles, and translates these principles into engineering strategies for designing exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers. We critically examine major biomimetic platforms such as cell membrane-coated nanoparticles, hybrid exosome-synthetic vesicles, lipid-based exosome mimetics, and polymeric biomimetic assemblies, with emphasis on fabrication techniques, drug loading approaches, targeting mechanisms, and advanced characterization methods. Recent therapeutic applications across oncology, central nervous system disorders, immunotherapy, gene and RNA delivery, and regenerative medicine are summarised with comparative insights into mechanistic performance. Furthermore, key challenges related to safety, manufacturing scalability, regulatory considerations, and quality control are discussed. Emerging trends, including microfluidic manufacturing, quality-by-design frameworks, and artificial intelligence-assisted nanocarrier optimization, are highlighted as future directions. Finally, we outline critical research gaps and propose a translational roadmap for clinical development of exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers.
